newsitem.title: UK: BA dispute tests new political climate.
newsitem.headline: BA dispute tests new political climate.

text.p: The confrontation between British Airways Plc management and its trades unions is the first litmus test of the industrial relations climate under a new Labour government, industry analysts said on Wednesday.

"There is an element of testing things out on both sides in this dispute. The unions are seeing whether the new political environment is favourable to them, while the company is trying to establish where it stands," said a senior industry analyst at a European investment bank.

The dispute, which threatens to disrupt flights during the peak summer season, pits BA chief executive Robert Ayling's tough-talking 1980s-style management -- trying to push through a one billion pound ($1.7 billion) restructuring -- against unions who say they have dumped their militant past and want to promote social partnership with industry.
Stuck in the middle is Tony Blair's new Labour government which has cultivated close connections with industry and in particular with Ayling, a friend of Blair.
"It's an old fashioned conflict between management and unions," said Ruth Lea, head of the Institute of Directors' policy unit.

"If Ayling thought he had an old Labour government in power he probably would not have behaved in this tough way, but new Labour, which has distanced itself from the unions and tried seriously to relate to business, must have been a factor in (Ayling's) equation," she said.

Despite its much-publicised pro-business rhetoric, Labour still retains strong cultural ties with its historical paymasters, the trades unions. So far the government has shown no interest in getting involved in this private sector dispute but it may be forced to take a position if it the strike takes place and begins to have a big effect.

"BA is such a big employer, this dispute is bound to indicate many things about the new Labour government. They can't just sit back and watch events like they're at a cricket match -- they may have to take sides" said John Kelly, senior lecturer in industrial relations at the London School of Economics (LSE).
The dispute with cabin crew is over pay and that with ground staff over the selling off of BA's catering division.
Most observers do not expect the government to intervene openly in the dispute.

But they agree that the Blair government's pro-business approach may have been misread by managers brought up under Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government which was responsible for bringing in tough laws restricting union activity in the 1980s.
"It's clear there has been a misinterpretation of new Labour's approach to unions," said Phil Woolaf, a Labour Member of Parliament with union connections.
"Companies have to understand that (social) partnership cuts both ways. New Labour wants management to work with the union but it would appear in this case this hasn't happened," he added.

The tough approach taken by BA -- threatening to sack or take legal action against individual employees who strike -- has reawakened fears among union leaders that BA is embarking on a new round of "union-bashing" -- a term much used by the left during Thatcher's regime.

"The new government's approach (through partnership)...risks being sabotaged by a high-profile dispute provoked by a company apparently incapable of getting the 1980s 'macho management' culture out of its system," said Bill Morris, general secretary of the Transport and General Workers Union, the main union involved in the BA conflict.

Ayling, who in turn has accused Morris of using "confrontational union behaviour of the worst sort", has said the airline intends to continue to operate flights despite the decision by cabin crew on Tuesday to go ahead with 72-hour strikes from next week.
The company has trained senior airline managers and other staff to work as substitute stewards and recruited hundreds of lorry-drivers, baggage handlers and loading staff at Heathrow Airport.

Such action would infuriate trade unionists and prompt comparisons with one of the darkest periods for modern British unions -- media tycoon Rupert Murdoch's decision in the mid-1980s to thwart striking printers by moving his News International printing operations to Wapping.
But, analysts say, British corporations will find they cannot run their businesses, particularly a public service firm like BA, without support from employees.
"You can run a company like a prison but you risk facing huge costs and a threat to the level of service. If you want success the key still seems to be rule by consent," said the LSE's Kelly.
